problem: Hedge 'It seems difficult' became flat 'It is hard'; 'attribute' became 'blame' (adds fault); 'may be assigned' dropped.
replacement: The first thing that strikes a traveler in the United States is the huge number of people trying to rise out of the condition they were born into. The second is how seldom one sees lofty ambition amid this restless, universal striving. Every American longs to get ahead, yet hardly any seem to cherish great hopes or to aim very high. All are constantly trying to gain property, power, and reputation, but few think of these things on a grand scale. This is all the more surprising because nothing in the customs or laws of America appears to hold desire back or to keep it from pressing outward in every direction. It seems hard to attribute this odd state of affairs to the equality of social conditions, since at the moment that same equality was established in France, ambition took flight without limit. Even so, I believe the chief cause that can be given for this fact lies in the social condition and the democratic customs of the Americans.

problem: Added 'academic' and 'of fitness' (not in source: 'probationary trial', 'taking honors').
replacement: In China, where equality of conditions is extreme and very ancient, no man moves from one public office to another without going through a probationary trial. This trial begins again at every stage of his career. The idea is by now so rooted in the customs of the people that I remember reading a Chinese novel in which the hero, after countless setbacks, finally wins his beloved’s heart by earning honors. Lofty ambition can hardly breathe in such an atmosphere.

problem: Ungrammatical 'holding it as undisturbed as an inherited fortune'; 'Suppose' framing is heavy. Fix grammar.
replacement: Suppose public employments are few, poorly paid, and insecure, while the various lines of business are numerous and profitable. Then the new and eager desires that the principle of equality produces turn from every side toward business, not toward official duties. But suppose that, while the ranks of society are growing more equal, the education of the people stays incomplete, or their spirit is anything but bold. Suppose commerce and industry, held back in their growth, offer only slow and difficult ways of making a fortune. Then the members of the community, despairing of improving their own condition, rush to the head of the state and demand its help. To relieve their own needs at the expense of the public treasury seems to them the easiest and most open way, if not the only one, to rise above a condition that no longer satisfies them. Place-hunting becomes the most widely followed of all trades. This must be especially so in those great centralized monarchies where paid offices are immensely numerous and the tenure of them fairly secure, so that no one despairs of getting a place and enjoying it as undisturbed as an inherited fortune.
